content.p: Pınarcık had no road. A German magazine reporter wrote a week after the attack that only a narrow footpath led from the hamlet, through tight valleys and along fast streams, to the next settlement eight kilometres away. Its Kurdish farmers kept goats and grew potatoes, and in winter the snow cut them off for months. On the evening of Saturday 20 June 1987 that isolation ended in gunfire and grenade blasts. By the end of the night, 30 people were dead according to Turkish officials, among them 16 children and six women. Der Spiegel counted 31.

All the victims were Kurds, Der Spiegel noted, like their attackers. The assault was carried out by guerrillas of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which was fighting the Turkish state, and it struck a hamlet where eight men served in the state-paid village guard system. The PKK's own magazine took credit for it. In 2011 a former policeman said the state itself was behind it, an account that others rejected.

Amnesty International, writing about the region in 1998, described the village guards as local auxiliaries armed and paid by the Turkish government to support the gendarmerie. Enrolment was voluntary in theory, it said, but the authorities viewed villagers who refused with suspicion, as possible PKK sympathisers. Those who declined were in many cases threatened, tortured, burned out of their villages, killed or made to disappear. Villages that accepted were exposed to a different danger, because the PKK, in its own publications, called guards agents of the state.

Pınarcık was such a village. Eight of its men were guards. A Turkish journalist who compiled attacks on guard families from the PKK's own published records put the hamlet at 16 households and 60 people. Der Spiegel called it the most terrible so far in a series of Kurdish attacks on Turkish soil. Only months earlier, it noted, a PKK unit had raided an Anatolian village and killed 14 people, and Turkey had answered by bombing Kurdish bases in neighbouring Iraq, killing at least 200 people.

The journalist's compilation places the assault at about 9:30 p.m. Accounts from the village describe an attack from three directions. Şeyhmus Yavuz, a retired guard who lived through it, told a news agency in 2017 that the fighters came in from three sides and that the guards held out until their ammunition ran out. He gave his age as 77 then and 86 when speaking to another agency in 2026. According to Turkish authorities, the shooting lasted more than two hours.

Survivors described houses being set on fire. A farmer interviewed by Der Spiegel said that he heard his children cry out to him to save them because they were being killed, and that his wife and six children were murdered. Yavuz, interviewed in 2017, said he lost 17 relatives, among them his wife and five children. Speaking in 2026 he listed his wife, five children, two brothers, a sister-in-law and nephews. He said that the attackers did not spare small children and that the livestock were burned as well. The sources do not reconcile every count, and the farmer in the German report may or may not be the same man.

The attackers left a leaflet in the hamlet. According to Der Spiegel, it described the dead as agents and servants of the fascist Turkish exploiters. A Turkish writer who quoted the text, signed by the PKK's armed wing, the ARGK, gave it as an order to surrender to the Kurdistan National Liberation Army, to ask the people's forgiveness and to answer for their crimes. The text, in the author's Turkish rendering, called the dead leaders of agent militia gangs.

The figure of 30 is the one repeated by Turkish officials. It appears in a 2026 memorial report from the district, in a Turkish parliament speech, in news agency anniversary pieces and in commentary, always with the breakdown of 16 children, six women and eight men. Der Spiegel, reporting within days, wrote that 31 villagers, 16 of them children, were killed. Michael Gunter, an American political scientist, wrote in 1991 of "some thirty civilians". Anadolu Agency's 2016 timeline gives the entry as "16 killed, including 16 children and 6 women", a line that contradicts itself, and the Daily Sabah timeline repeats it. The 30 given elsewhere is consistent in its breakdown.

The parliamentary speech, delivered by Halil Özşavlı, a member from Şanlıurfa, also said that the press at the time ran the headline "Haberli katliam" (roughly, a massacre announced in advance) with pictures of dead toddlers. He used the case to argue that civilian victims of PKK violence were forgotten, and said that most of the civilians the PKK killed were Kurds.

The June 1987 issue of the PKK's magazine Serxwebun, as quoted by a Turkish news agency, called the attack a "noble action" that revealed "facts that no one can distort". The same piece, translated here, said a team of 80 ARGK fighters surrounded the village and "the gangs were destroyed". Another Turkish writer quoted the magazine as calling it the culmination of a series of actions, after which the fascist army and special units had fallen into fear.

The same writer recorded that the magazine went on to claim raids on the villages of Peçenek and Yuvalı in early July, which it said happened while Prime Minister Turgut Özal was visiting Pınarcık. Anadolu Agency's timeline dates a Peçenek attack to 8 July and lists 16 dead there, while the writer dated the Haraberk raid in Yuvalı to 10 July with nine dead. Years later, the same writer noted, PKK figures including Murat Karayılan and Cemil Bayık said that raids on guards' villages at the end of the 1980s had been mistakes, while the magazine had boasted of them at the time. A columnist for a Turkish newspaper quoted Abdullah Öcalan as saying after Pınarcık, in this translation, that they should kill and so become the authority. That wording comes from a partisan column and the opened pages give no date or setting for it.

The attack came a day or two after the European Parliament adopted a resolution saying that Turkey's refusal to recognise the Armenian genocide and the Kurdish question were "insurmountable obstacles" to considering it for membership of the European Community. Turkish President Kenan Evren blamed the resolution for encouraging the PKK, and threatened to punish those responsible the day after tomorrow if not tomorrow. Der Spiegel called the claim hardly serious. Gunter wrote that Evren's accusation had "some merit" and had come two days after the resolution.

The Turkish news agency Hürriyet claimed the attackers came from Syria, whose border was about 25 kilometres from the hamlet, Der Spiegel reported, and noted that Turkey had no cross-border pursuit agreement with Damascus as it had with Iraq. In July 1987 Özal signed a security protocol in Damascus under which Syria agreed to stop the PKK raiding Turkey from its territory and to remove its camps, according to Gunter.

In March 2011 Ayhan Çarkın, a former police special-operations officer who had served in the south-east from 1986 and had been convicted at the Susurluk trial of membership of a gang, told two newspapers that many massacres, Pınarcık among them, had been carried out by JİTEM, the gendarmerie's intelligence unit, not by the PKK. Bianet reported that he also referred to the well-known photograph of a shot baby as having been taken at Pınarcık. The journalist Celal Başlangıç called the claim important if made by a former state official. Others were sceptical: the activist Şanar Yurdatapan said Çarkın contradicted himself and could not be taken at face value.

In March 2011 Çarkın also said he had taken part in Pınarcık, Başbağlar and several other massacres, and he was arrested in June. He had said on television in 2008 that he might have killed a thousand people. In his later statement to the Diyarbakır prosecutor, Bianet reported, he weakened the value of his earlier claims. Separately, when the court in the Ankara JİTEM case acquitted all defendants in December 2019, the prosecutor described Çarkın's statements in that case as contradictory. That trial concerned 19 killings and disappearances, not Pınarcık. The opened pages do not show any court establishing who committed the 1987 killings.

A cemetery for the victims lies in the hamlet. In June 2026, on the 39th anniversary, the Ömerli district governor, the mayor, security chiefs and the head of a confederation of village guards and martyrs' families laid roses at the graves. The mayor said that the people there hoped that the process Turkey calls Terror-Free Türkiye would spare others such pain. Yavuz, by then 86, told reporters, in translation, that he sees it all before his eyes and does not forget.
